recent_commits.message: Checks after data_check name a repository refused for its number of files (#706); faults from the Meta-Psychology run (#695 points 41, 32), #593 points 1 and 3, #590. Version 0.4.4.32
recent_commits.body:
- data_check returns the repositories it refused for max_files_per_repo as count_refused; code_check, codebook_check, psychds_check and reproducibility_check name them and are yellow (code_check said "0 code files" for zenodo.3826426).
- reproducibility_check no longer stops with "non-character argument" when code_check's files_written holds only NA (a paper with only a JASP file, mp20202538).
- codebook_check's model step no longer matches a column to a codebook variable without a label.
- A script that stopped at its own check of the number of command-line arguments, or that indexes args it never assigns, is needs_a_person.
- Python 2 code gets the packages of the local modules it imports (.repro_py_with_imports()).
- Of several different same-named deposit files, the one whose folders match the path the script asked for is copied (.repro_path_tail_match()).

Checked on seven BES papers with Docker: 14340 runs 5 scripts instead of 2; the argument scripts of 14155 and 13721 are needs_a_person; numpy is installed for Python 2 in 13324.
recent_commits.author: Lakens

recent_commits.message: Fixes for #700, #702 and #703: large, damaged and unusual repositories. Version 0.4.4.30
recent_commits.body:
#703: a damaged archive that cannot be opened is reported, not silently dropped; data_check and codebook_check no longer fail on empty tables; a tree whose files all sit in a junk folder is drawn correctly.
#702: the file tree, path grouping, lowercasing of long texts and package detection take time in proportion to the number of files; the tree is cut at 2,000 lines; max_files_per_repo defaults to 100,000, and data_check and code_check refuse larger repositories early with a message.

recent_commits.message: Download limits, parts 2 and 3 of #699: one choice of files per repository for the whole run, code_check's zips within the budget, archives unpacked within the budget. Version 0.4.4.29
recent_commits.body:
- download_repo_files() chooses each repository's files once from its full listing (repo_listing, passed by every check), so the checks together keep a repository within one max_download_size; the folder's contents count first, files unpacked from archives at their unpacked size.
- .code_expand_zip() fetches its code files through download_repo_files().
- data_check unpacks zip, tar and .gz files only within what is left of the budget, and leaves out archives in renv folders.
- .safe_write_path() gains root: a long path is shortened below the repository's folder only, so archive files are no longer stored in a second folder the budget did not count.
- A repository over max_files_per_repo has no files fetched from its archives either.
- The platform *_file_download() functions default to 100 MB per file and 500 MB in total.
recent_commits.author: Lakens

recent_commits.message: Download limits, first part of #699: no download path without a limit; ResearchBox held to the limits; GEO, ENA and ArrayExpress records whose archive did not answer are "unreachable", not "unfound". Version 0.4.4.28
recent_commits.body:
- download_repo_files() names each file a limit left out, with the reason, in a new attribute "limit_refused". code_check does not read such a file from the web; any other code file read from the web is fetched through .download_capped() and stops at max_file_size. A code file inside an archive is no longer requested from the address "NA" with download = FALSE.
- reproducibility_check passes max_file_size and max_download_size to the code_check it runs.
- .tar_fetch_members() stops an archive of unknown size at what is left of the budget.
- ResearchBox: repo_check (and data_check and code_check, which pass them on) and rbox_file_download() have max_file_size and max_download_size. With an API key the file list is asked first and only the smallest files up to the budget are downloaded; without a key the download stops at the budget and the box is reported as not downloaded. .download_capped() takes a prepared request.
- The message about files over max_file_size rounds the largest size up to 0.1 MB.
- seq_archive_info(): .seq_fetch() tells an archive that did not answer from one that has no such record.
- Documentation corrected: a file of unknown size is downloaded up to a limit, not skipped; osf_file_download()'s default mode is "all", without limits; download_repo_files()'s budget counts only the files of one call.

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): the cross-reference A/B is unresolved; it stays off by default
recent_commits.body:
Five baseline swarm runs on psi: 3, 5, 5, 5, 7 of 16, precision 100% every
time. Two cross-reference runs: 5 and 8 of 16, precision 87% and 100%.

The pre-registered rule was that recall must rise outside the baseline range
and precision must not fall. Precision fell in one of the two runs against
100% in five of five, so the rule is not met and the round is not shipped on.
rounds=1 stays the default.

The result is ambiguous rather than negative, and that is reported as such.
The 8 of 16 is the highest recall any swarm run has reached, above the
baseline ceiling, at unchanged precision; two observations against five with a
baseline spread of 3 to 7 cannot separate it from variance. The code stays
behind rounds=2, off, rather than being deleted: one run at the best recall
yet is worth someone's attention and one precision failure is worth nobody's
trust. Settling it needs about four more runs per arm.

The failing run is diagnosed: a round-1 claim about sigma-hat dependency went
onto the board and came back written up twice, as a comment and as an issue,
and the adjudicator rejects both because the scores and the noise carry the
same scale factor so selection is invariant to it. The refuter confirmed all
eight candidates in that run, so the gate built as the defence against a claim
spreading undemonstrated did not catch it. That bounds how far that gate can
be trusted elsewhere in this design and is recorded separately.

recent_commits.message: feat(agent): add a cross-reference round over a shared findings board
recent_commits.body:
Targets the swarm's one measured deficiency, which is coverage rather than
precision: three to nine comments against references holding 16 and 25
findings, at precision the staged pipeline cannot match. Its investigators
work in complete isolation, so one checking an appendix proof never learns
that another found the same quantity treated differently in the main text --
the exact shape of the cross-location findings this harness exists to recover.

With rounds=2, the orchestrator writes a digest of every candidate finding to
the workspace and re-runs each investigator with it, asking what those leads
imply for its own part of the paper. The board carries ids, titles, locations
and one-line claims and nothing of the reasoning or computation behind them,
and it is written by the orchestrator rather than by the agents: an agent
shown another's derivation audits the derivation instead of the paper, which
is the distinction the whole independent-refuter design rests on. The brief
forbids repeating, citing or relying on an entry, and everything the round
produces still passes the independent refuter.

rounds=1 is the default and leaves the existing path untouched, so this is an
A/B rather than a replacement: agent_swarm against agent_swarm_xref in the
eval harness. Whether it actually raises recall without costing precision is
measured next; if it costs precision it comes out.

Also splits the five role agents into coarse/agent/roles.py, which keeps
orchestrator under the size cap. That split matters for _refute in
particular: it is deliberately given the claim and the paper and NOT the
investigator's reasoning, and the omission is easier to see when the function
is not buried in the flow that produced the claim.

recent_commits.message: feat(agent): ship --refute for comments only; remove the macro-issue half
recent_commits.body:
The macro-issue gate was built, measured on three papers, and does not earn
its place. On psi it converted no unsupported issue and dropped a supported
one. On coset_codes its entire upside was two issues flipping to supported
when their narrowed text was re-judged, by a judge already observed to change
verdict on byte-identical text.

Reading the narrowed output settled it. An issue titled 'Multiplicity formulas
rest on unverified uniformity assumptions' came back with a body saying the
assumption 'holds for the partitions checked here ... which reproduces the
table's 44, 252, 764 and 316': the deletion had removed the criticism and left
text confirming the assumption, under a title still asserting the defect. A
gate that can leave a heading contradicting its own paragraph should not run on
an author-facing review.

Removes refute_issues, _refute_issue, narrow_by_deletion and its whitespace
helpers, IssueVerdict, refute_review, the issue-refuter prompt, and their
tests. The pipeline calls refute_comments directly. The overall feedback now
passes through the stage untouched, which a pipeline-level test asserts.

The removed code is in this branch's history if it is worth revisiting with
more papers and a verdict-stable judge.

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): report the gate gross, add the coverage check, drop an unsupported claim
recent_commits.body:
Three corrections to how the result is stated.

The headline was net. Gross it is 9 bad comments dropped, 3 good claims
dropped, and 2 bad issues that became good when their narrowed text was
re-judged — so the macro-issue half's entire upside is two re-judgements by a
judge that has changed verdict on byte-identical text, which is what this
measurement otherwise excludes.

'Keeps the pipeline's coverage' was asserted, not measured. Crossing each
reference finding's matching claim against what the gate did to it: no finding
on any of the three papers was carried by a claim the gate dropped. Eight ride
on a narrowed claim, which re-scoring recall would settle and which has not
been done.

'Making the gate subtractive made it reproducible' is withdrawn. It rested on
two runs compared by counts, the second overwrote the first's per-claim record,
and the comment refuter's prompt and drop rule did not change, so the redesign
cannot be the cause.

Also: the Design bullet for --refute described comments only, the CHANGELOG
still said a comment is rewritten when misstated, and two caveats were missing
(the all-refuted notice is English only; nobody has read a deletion-narrowed
issue end to end).

narrowed issue lost its paragraph breaks and the newlines inside display math,
turning it into one run-on block. That damaged the issue whether or not the
deletion itself was right, and 15 of 35 issues across the benchmark papers
were narrowed.

Whitespace is now tidied only where a span was removed: a deletion that
spanned a paragraph boundary keeps the break, one inside a paragraph leaves a
single space, and display math is untouched. Tests cover the paragraph,
inline, display-math, rewrapped and trailing cases.

refute_effect.py now also saves the post-refutation review and each narrowed

says, so no one could read one for a dangling fragment or a lost antecedent.

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): final refutation measurement on three papers
recent_commits.body:
Measured on identical generation with stored verdicts carried forward for
untouched claims, reported as good and bad counts under the stricter
supported-and-substantive test.

Across psi, the held-out coset_codes, and targeting: 11 bad claims removed
against 1 good one lost, at about $1.85 a paper.

Three findings that matter more than the total, and one of them reverses this
document's previous claim:

- The comment half carries the benefit (9 bad removed, 2 good lost). The
  macro-issue half is marginal (2 bad removed, 1 good gained) and was net
  negative on psi, converting no bad issue and dropping a good one. The
  earlier claim that the issue half 'mattered most' came from the retracted
  measurements and does not survive them.
- On targeting, the only paper no design decision here has touched and whose
  review was already 26 good to 6 bad, the gate dropped nothing and changed no
  verdict. The right failure mode, but it means the value depends on the paper.
- Making the gate subtractive made it reproducible: two genuine psi runs agree
  exactly, where the rewriting version dropped 4, then 5, then 6 of the same
  comments.

The recommendation stays opt-in, and now names the macro-issue half as the
open question rather than the main gain.

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): withdraw the refutation figures and record why they were wrong
recent_commits.body:
Three successive attempts at what the gate is worth were each wrong: comparing
two different pipeline runs, re-judging unchanged text through a judge that
drifts, and scoring an is-this-supported test that a hedged rewrite satisfies.
The third changed the design rather than the measurement.

The doc now states the withdrawal, the three mistakes, and the shape that
survived all of them, rather than a number. It no longer recommends
considering --refute as a default.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix(agent): make the refutation gate purely subtractive
recent_commits.body:
Reading the saved reviews showed the gate was rewriting the review, not
verifying it, and that this was the source of its own measured gain.

Issues: asking for a replacement body produced a rewrite longer than the
original on every narrowed issue across both benchmark papers (1.0x to 1.6x),
each prefixed with the issue title. Refusing those by length left the issue
half drop-only, which pays nothing; accepting them made an agent the author of
review prose. Narrowing is now expressed as deletion: the refuter names
verbatim spans of the body that the paper does not bear out, and the code
removes them, so every surviving word is the reviewer's own. Matching is exact
then whitespace-insensitive, since a model re-wraps a sentence it quotes; a
span that still does not match removes nothing, so a hallucinated span cannot
alter the issue, and naming every span drops the issue outright.

Comments: corrected_claim is no longer applied. Sampling the rewrites found
ones that retreated from 'X is wrong' to 'the paper does not say how X was
handled', which satisfies an is-this-supported test while giving the author
less -- so part of the measured precision gain was an artefact of the metric.
The suggestion stays on the verdict for a human to weigh. severity is now only
ever lowered: the field defaults to 'major', so applying it unconditionally
raised the severity of comments the refuter never reconsidered.

Because the gate now only removes, every surviving comment keeps the verdict
already stored for it and the effect measurement needs no re-judging except
for narrowed issue bodies. refute_effect.py reports good and bad counts rather
than rates, and records per-claim what the gate did.

Refutation tests move to tests/test_agent_refutation.py beside their module.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix(agent): make narrowing actually narrow, and key comments by position
recent_commits.body:
Three defects, two of them found by reading the saved reviews rather than the
verdicts.

refute_comments keyed its lookup maps on comment.number. This stage runs
before _renumber_comments, so the numbers are whatever the editorial pass
emitted, and on the double-failure fallback path they are raw section order
with section-local numbering where duplicates are expected. Comments sharing a
number collapsed the maps and had verdicts misattributed. Keyed on position
now, as the issue path already was.

Every narrowed issue body on the benchmark papers came back LONGER than the
one it replaced, against the prompt's explicit instruction to say less and
never more, and each began by repeating the issue title so the rendered review
showed the title twice. A prompt cannot enforce either. _clean_narrowed_body
strips a repeated title and refuses a body that does not shorten, keeping the
original instead: a rewrite that expands makes this stage an author of review
content rather than a verifier of it, which is the risk the ledger link
elsewhere exists to prevent.

The review language now reaches both refuters. A refuter writes author-facing
prose (corrected_claim, rewritten_body), and the issue refuter rewrites most
of what it touches, so without this the rewrite came back in English inside a
localized review. The all-issues-refuted notice is still English; that is
recorded as a caveat.

Adds a pipeline-level test for review_paper(refute=True), which the benchmark
never exercised because it called refute_comments and refute_issues directly.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): measure the refutation gate on identical generation
recent_commits.body:
refute_saved.py now also refutes the macro issues and can save what survives
as its own run, so precision before and after is compared on the same
generation rather than across two pipeline runs.

With both halves refuted, on psi and on the held-out coset_codes: unsupported
claims halve (10 to 4, and 16 to 8), precision rises 19 and 17 points, recall
is unchanged on one paper and loses one finding of 25 on the other, and the
pass costs about $1.85. Issue precision, the gap the comment-only version
left at 58% and 36%, reaches 80% and 50%.

The per-claim cross-tabulation shows why the two halves need separate
contracts: the gate drops 8 of 14 false comments for 2 of 25 good ones, while
on issues it narrows 12 of 23 rather than dropping them, and the narrowed text
is what the precision gain is measured on. Two caveats are stated with it: the
refuter has real run-to-run variance, and it also narrowed 6 issues the judge
had called supported, so the trade is net positive on these two papers rather
than free.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: feat(agent): refute the macro issues too, narrowing rather than dropping
recent_commits.body:
With comments alone refuted, comment precision reached 94% and 100% on the two
benchmark papers while macro-issue precision stayed at 58% and 36%, so every
surviving unsupported claim was in the overall feedback.

A macro issue is not a comment and needs a different contract. It carries no
verbatim anchor, so the refuter locates the passages itself. And it bundles
several points under one theme, so the common outcome is that some hold and
some do not: dropping a four-point issue because its third point is answered
in Section 6 discards three good ones, while keeping it whole ships the wrong
one. IssueVerdict therefore adds 'partly_supported', which replaces the body
with the reviewer's narrowed version and records what was dropped and where
the paper answers it. The title survives narrowing.

Guards: an issue is kept unchanged when the check could not run or came back
inconclusive, so neither an infrastructure failure nor honest uncertainty
deletes one; a narrowing with no replacement text keeps the original, since
the reviewer called it partly right; and if every issue is refuted, an
explicit notice replaces them rather than reinstating the least-bad one,
because OverviewFeedback requires an issue and the least-bad one is still a
claim the paper contradicts.

refute_review is now the single entry point the pipeline stage calls, with the
two halves failing independently so a failure in one leaves the other verified.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: refactor(agent): split the pipeline-facing refutation gate into its own module
recent_commits.body:
orchestrator.py reached 804 lines, over the architecture cap. refute_comments
is the natural seam: orchestrator holds the roles and modes, refutation holds
the gate applied to comments produced outside them, which the measurement made
the primary use. 702 and 127 lines.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix: validate the agent mode, and don't drop a substantive 'Funding' section
recent_commits.body:
run_agentic_review fell through to swarm for any unrecognized mode, so a typo
in --agent silently ran a different and dearer mode; it now raises.

Section eligibility skipped any title starting with a boilerplate word, which
would discard an economics paper's 'Funding and acquisition dynamics in
venture capital'. The prefix test now applies only to headings short enough to
be that boilerplate.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): rewrite from the paired refutation measurement
recent_commits.body:
The refutation result was unpaired: pipeline_refuted was a separate pipeline
run, so comparing it with the pipeline arm compared two different reviews.
evals/refute_saved.py now runs the refuter over the exact comments the judge
already adjudicated, one paired observation per comment. The honest figure is
much smaller than the one that was published here: comment precision 64% to
82% across the two papers, the gate dropping 9 of 14 false criticisms and 2 of
25 good ones, and the two papers differing a great deal.

Also: the design section listed two tools that do not exist (web_search,
finding_write) and omitted that there is no web search and only one refutation
pass; the tool-judge result is now described as consistent with the diagnosis
rather than confirming it, since its prompt names the hypothesis; the host
isolation section no longer describes a particular machine's configuration;
and a closing section states plainly where the work departs from what was
asked.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: docs: correct module descriptions and the section-fix changelog entry
recent_commits.body:
The seven module descriptions added to the package-structure tables were
written from the file names rather than from the modules. Checked against each
docstring: handoff_url only parses (it does not construct, and nothing is
signed), native_runtime suspends model calls as native tasks and replays
validated responses rather than detecting and launching a runtime, and
native_review and review_runtime were also inaccurate. All seven now follow
their docstrings.

The changelog claimed the fix makes the pipeline review every section. It does
not: the cap still binds on a long paper, and the entry now says which
sections are dropped and that the choice is logged.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix(agent): enforce sandbox network denial at the OS level
recent_commits.body:
The 'no network' claim was false. Denial was a Python-level patch of the
socket module, and two one-liners defeated it: subprocess shelling out to
/usr/bin/curl returned HTTP 200, and 'import _socket' connected directly,
since the patch only touches the pure-Python wrapper. A paper is untrusted
input, so a prompt-injected paper that induced the model to write an
exfiltrating check would have had a working path out.

Denial now comes from the OS where a mechanism exists: sandbox-exec with a
deny-network seatbelt profile on macOS, 'unshare --net' on Linux where
permitted. Both are probed by actually running them, because either can be
present and refuse. Verified on this host: the curl bypass now exits 6 and
_socket cannot connect, while sympy still imports and runs.

Where no mechanism is available there is no network bound, and nothing now
claims otherwise: available_isolation() reports the mechanism, and the python
tool's description is generated from it, so a host without isolation tells the
model so instead of giving it a false assurance. The socket patch stays as a
legible error message rather than a bound, and both bypasses are now tests.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): final arm comparison, with a tool-using second adjudication
recent_commits.body:
Adds the refuted-pipeline arms, which validate the recommendation: refutation
took detailed-comment precision from 58% to 100% on the held-out paper and
from 70% to 94% on the other. It also shows where the remaining false
criticism is — entirely in the macro issues, which the stage does not yet
refute.

Adds evals/adjudicate.py, a second audit by a judge with the same workspace
and tools the agents get, because the single-prompt judge never abstained and
was being asked to check lookups it had no means to perform. It is more
lenient, so the single-prompt precision figures were too harsh and are now
reported alongside it. It confirms the mechanism far more firmly: five of the
six unsupported claims it found are objections the paper answers elsewhere,
and it names the location each time.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: chore(evals): keep benchmark inputs out of the repository
recent_commits.body:
structure.json embeds the whole paper text while paper.md was ignored, which
was an inconsistent policy for the same content, and the reference reviews are
third-party documents. evals/papers/ is now ignored in full. What stays
committed is the atomized finding sets under evals/references/ and
prepare_paper.py, which regenerates the rest from a local PDF.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): full arm comparison across two papers, with the leakage caveat
recent_commits.body:
Replaces the single-paper table with both papers and all arms, and states the
leakage plainly: the role prompts were written after reading the first paper's
reference review and name the patterns it found, so recall on that paper is
in-sample and the held-out paper is the honest measurement.

The recommendation follows what was measured rather than the premise the
branch started from: the staged pipeline leads on coverage and asserts the
most unsupported claims, the agent arms reverse both, so verification is added
to the generator instead of replacing it.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: feat(pipeline): add --refute, an independent re-check of every comment
recent_commits.body:
The arm comparison measured generation and verification as complements, not
substitutes. On both benchmark papers the staged pipeline was the coverage
leader and also asserted the most claims the paper does not support: 15 of 32
on one, 16 of 31 on the other, roughly half. The agent arms reversed both,
asserting almost nothing unsupported while finding far too little.

So rather than replacing the staged pipeline, refute_comments applies the
agent runtime's gate to the comments it already produced. Each one goes to a
fresh-context agent that sees the claim and its quote, has tool access to the
whole paper, and must reproduce the defect; a comment it cannot reproduce is
dropped, and one that is real but misstated is rewritten from the refuter's
corrected claim. A comment whose check could not run is kept, so an
infrastructure failure never silently deletes a finding.

Exposed as review_paper(refute=True) and 'coarse review --refute', off by
default, with a pipeline_refuted evaluation arm.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: feat(cli): add --agent to run a review through the bounded agent runtime
recent_commits.body:
Until now the agent runtime had no entry point: review_paper always ran the
staged pipeline, so the whole package was unreachable from the CLI or the
library. review_paper takes agent_mode (sweep|swarm|single) and `coarse
review --agent <mode>` sets it. Default None, so the staged path is
unchanged.

The agent branch reuses the shared quote verifier and renderer rather than
its own, so the verbatim-quote guarantee is identical on both paths; a test
covers that a fabricated quote is still dropped from an agent review.

pipeline.py joins the oversized-module allowlist at 880 lines. Moving the
quote-repair helpers to review_stages.py would have kept it under the cap but
broke 22 tests that patch those names on coarse.pipeline, so that refactor
belongs in its own change rather than riding along here.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: chore(tests): record the prompts.py cap bump for the sweep brief
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: feat(agent): add sweep mode — broad coverage behind the refutation gate
recent_commits.body:
Measured separately on the benchmark paper, the two capabilities were
complementary rather than competing. A single full-paper pass reached nine of
sixteen reference findings but asserted one the paper does not support. The
role swarm asserted nothing unsupported across three runs, and reached two
appendix findings nothing else reached (a one-sided premise in a composition
lemma, and a curvature bound off by a factor of two), but only three to five
findings in total: narrow targets do not cover a paper.

Sweep divides every reviewable section into contiguous regions, one per
investigator, and briefs each for breadth rather than for a single question --
same demonstration bar, but abstention is no longer the expected outcome. Every
candidate still passes through an independent fresh-context refuter before the
editor sees it. The brief also tells a sweeper to search the rest of the paper
before reporting that something is missing, which is the failure that produced
every unsupported comment in the pipeline arm.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix(agent): require the planner to name at least one target
recent_commits.body:
The planner submitted an empty plan on every run, after seven turns and ten
of its thirty-five permitted tool calls, so it was not running out of budget:
InvestigationPlan simply allowed an empty list, and an empty submission
validated. The orchestrator then fell back to structural targets and the
LLM plan was never used.

An empty plan is never a useful answer, unlike an empty FindingBatch where
abstention is the point. Requiring a target makes the empty submission fail
validation, which the runner already feeds back to the agent as a rejection
to repair.

Also adds evals/prepare_paper.py, which extracts a held-out paper, analyzes
its structure and atomizes its reference review mechanically (one finding per
macro issue and per detailed comment). Needed because the role prompts were
written after reading the first paper's reference review and name the patterns
that review found, so recall on that paper is in-sample and cannot support a
quality claim on its own.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix(agent,evals): enforce the ledger link in code and audit macro issues too
recent_commits.body:
Two measurement and safety gaps the first arm comparison exposed.

The editor was told to write only from confirmed findings but nothing checked
it. Each detailed comment now carries the finding id it reports, and a comment
whose id is not in the confirmed set is dropped, so a finding an independent
refuter did not reproduce cannot re-enter the report through the editor. When
the editor attributes nothing at all the comments are kept and the degradation
is logged, rather than discarding a whole report over a missing field.

Precision was adjudicated over detailed comments only while recall credited
macro issues as well, so an arm that put its claims in the overall feedback
was credited for hits and never charged for misses. On the benchmark paper
that asymmetry mattered a great deal: the whole of one arm's measured recall
came from its macro issues and none of its 21 detailed comments matched a
reference finding. Both halves of a review are now adjudicated, and recall
reports how many hits came from a detailed comment rather than only from a
macro issue.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: chore(evals): untrack local benchmark run logs
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: fix(pipeline): keep a proof whose title the heading parser mangled
recent_commits.body:
Section eligibility filtered on the title, dropping any section titled
`<!-- PAGE BREAK -->`. When a page break falls immediately before a heading
the parser uses the marker as the title and leaves the real heading in the
body, so such a section can hold real content: on the benchmark paper one is
1,107 characters of "A.6 Proof of Theorem 2", the proof of the paper's
central result, and the reference review's critical finding is about a step
in it.

Eligibility is now judged on the text alone. The underlying mis-titling in
structure.py is untouched.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: chore(evals): ignore local benchmark run logs
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: docs(agent): record the measured arm comparison
recent_commits.body:
The pipeline matched a plain one-prompt baseline's recall while emitting seven
criticisms the adjudicator found unsupported, and all seven fail for the same
reason: the objection is answered elsewhere in the paper, where a
single-section prompt cannot see it.
recent_commits.author: David Van Dijcke

recent_commits.message: Label pre-check: see through a trailing parenthetical
recent_commits.body:
"Experiment 2 (Sample 1)" hid the study token from the end-anchored
_LABEL_TOKEN_RE, so the pre-check declared the label absent and skipped
isolation on a genuinely two-experiment paper. Match the bare label
(parenthetical stripped) and extract the token from it as well.
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Bump Authlib 1.7.2 -> 1.9.1 for new security advisories
recent_commits.body:
CI's dependency audit started failing on eight advisories published
against Authlib 1.7.2 (PYSEC-2026-4354..4360, CVE-2026-96760,
CVE-2026-116672); 1.9.1 fixes all of them. Only authlib changes in the
hash-locked requirements.lock.
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Match target studies whose labels carry a title
recent_commits.body:
A real gpt-5.5 run on Yu et al. (2024) labelled studies as
'Study 4: Feeling Gratitude Toward Close Versus Distant Others'; the
trailing-token match found no number, so 'Study 4' resolved to nothing
and isolation fell back to the generative method. The study number is
now taken from 'Study/Experiment N' anywhere in the label first.
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Label-based multi-study isolation in production
recent_commits.body:
Isolation now defaults to the label method prototyped in
benchmarks/parser_eval/study_labels.py: one experiment-model call labels
every paragraph and sentence of the paper by study (labels only, no
text), and the target study's text is assembled deterministically from
the paper's own sentences (shared + target units, in order). Text is
verbatim, so nothing is paraphrased or dropped by regeneration; sentences
imported through a cross-reference carry a short
'[From Study X, cited for: <aspect>]' prefix, and the judge prompt now
says the target's own text takes precedence over imported lines.

New backend/services/study_labels.py holds the pure parts: a segmenter
that also handles PDF text layers (hard wraps, no blank lines, heading
lines, tables), the labelling prompt, label validation, target matching
("2" / "Study 2" / "Experiment 2" / single-study papers) and the filter.
On the CLI the labels are cached per paper, so every study of a paper
reuses one labelling call.

extract_experiment_specific_paper_text dispatches by method
(ISOLATION_METHOD, default labels) and falls back to the generative
rewrite when labelling fails; results and Redis record
multi_study_isolation_method and the fallback reason. Multi-study and
supplement runs now build the paper evidence from the original document,
with isolated chunks placed on its pages by word alignment.
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: One canonical text per document
recent_commits.body:
The selected parser's output is now the single text the judge, retrieval
and the evidence text pane use. Previously, whenever the evidence viewer
was built (every web run), PDFs were re-chunked from PyMuPDF's text
layer and that text replaced the parser output, so GROBID/DPT2/bibr
results never reached the judge and partially scanned PDFs lost their
OCR. build_pdf_evidence_source now chunks the parser text and places each
chunk on the pages by aligning its words to the PDF word stream
(_DocumentWords: tolerant of running heads, page numbers and page
breaks); unplaceable chunks carry no offsets so the viewer searches
instead. Without parser text the text layer stays canonical.

Corpora built without the evidence viewer (plain CLI, eval scripts,
lazy builds in run_comparison) now use corpus_segments, the same
chunking, display normalisation and reference flags as the evidence
builder, so both paths embed identical segments. PDF registrations get
the same clean_document_text pass as other formats; number-only lines
are dropped only for PDF-derived text (an OSF answer of "300" was being
deleted). Corpus truncation at MAX_EMBEDDING_SEGMENTS is now logged.
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Judge independent dimensions in parallel
recent_commits.body:
All three orchestrators now dispatch dimensions through one helper,
_judge_dimensions. Without --append-previous-output the dimensions are
independent and run concurrently (DIMENSION_CONCURRENCY, default 4, per
job); partial and final results stay in dimension order. With the append
chain they run strictly in sequence as before.

Corpora are built once before fan-out (_ensure_text_corpora), which also
stops consensus strands from embedding the same documents once per
voter; the lazily-built full-paper corpus is guarded by a lock. Because
parallel threads write relevance scores into the shared evidence
manifest, it is persisted once after the dimensions finish (and per
dimension only in the sequential case).
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Worker: oldest-first queue, independent heartbeat, evidence off the loop
recent_commits.body:
Producers now LPUSH and the worker keeps popping the tail (BRPOPLPUSH),
so jobs run first-in-first-out; jobs reclaimed from a dead worker are
RPUSHed to the tail and run next. The heartbeat is refreshed by its own
task every TTL/3 instead of once per dequeue iteration, which stalled
while all job slots were busy and let a peer reclaim (and re-run) live
jobs. The orchestrators' synchronous evidence building and corpus
embedding now run via asyncio.to_thread so they no longer block the
event loop (and with it the heartbeat and other jobs).
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Keep supplements out of the references section; fix label-not-found framing
recent_commits.body:
Supplementary material appended after a paper's reference list was
flagged in_references and dropped from retrieval, disabling --supplement.
The references span now ends at the next merged-document separator
(DOCUMENT_SEPARATOR_RE), in both the evidence-builder flags and the
heading fallback in _reference_chunk_ids, and the separator line is a
chunk boundary.

For label_not_found_full_text runs the judge was told the paper reports
several studies and was pre-filtered; it now gets a variant that says the
label is absent, the excerpts are unfiltered, and the paper may report a
single study.
recent_commits.author: Jamie Cummins

recent_commits.message: Surface supplement references; add --supplement to the CLI
recent_commits.body:
Detect references to supplementary material in the paper body
(supplement/supplemental/supplementary, supporting information, online

highlights.message: docs(agent): the cross-reference A/B is unresolved; it stays off by default
highlights.body:
Five baseline swarm runs on psi: 3, 5, 5, 5, 7 of 16, precision 100% every
time. Two cross-reference runs: 5 and 8 of 16, precision 87% and 100%.

The pre-registered rule was that recall must rise outside the baseline range
and precision must not fall. Precision fell in one of the two runs against
100% in five of five, so the rule is not met and the round is not shipped on.
rounds=1 stays the default.

The result is ambiguous rather than negative, and that is reported as such.
The 8 of 16 is the highest recall any swarm run has reached, above the
baseline ceiling, at unchanged precision; two observations against five with a
baseline spread of 3 to 7 cannot separate it from variance. The code stays
behind rounds=2, off, rather than being deleted: one run at the best recall
yet is worth someone's attention and one precision failure is worth nobody's
trust. Settling it needs about four more runs per arm.

The failing run is diagnosed: a round-1 claim about sigma-hat dependency went
onto the board and came back written up twice, as a comment and as an issue,
and the adjudicator rejects both because the scores and the noise carry the
same scale factor so selection is invariant to it. The refuter confirmed all
eight candidates in that run, so the gate built as the defence against a claim
spreading undemonstrated did not catch it. That bounds how far that gate can
be trusted elsewhere in this design and is recorded separately.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): the cross-reference round failed its pre-registered test
highlights.body:
Decision rule set before the numbers: recall must rise outside the baseline
range and precision must not fall. On psi, one run each on identical code:
recall 5/16 both ways, and precision 100% -> 87% with 2 unsupported claims.
Output volume nearly tripled, 4 comments to 11, for no new coverage. The
matched sets differ by a swap, not a gain: D5 picked up, O4a lost.

The mechanism does work in isolation. Three of eight candidates came from the
second round and two are real reference findings, D5 and D6. What sank it is
that a round-1 claim about sigma-hat dependency went onto the board and came
back written up twice, as a comment and as an issue, and the adjudicator
rejects both because the scores and the noise are scaled by the same factor so
the selection is invariant to it.

The refuter confirmed all eight candidates. The gate built specifically as the
defence against a claim spreading without being demonstrated did not catch
this one, which is worth recording separately from the round's own failure.

coset_codes cannot resolve the question: its swarm recall is 1/25 and 2/25
across runs, structurally capped by a reference whose items are mostly reading
difficulties rather than defects.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: feat(agent): add a cross-reference round over a shared findings board
highlights.body:
Targets the swarm's one measured deficiency, which is coverage rather than
precision: three to nine comments against references holding 16 and 25
findings, at precision the staged pipeline cannot match. Its investigators
work in complete isolation, so one checking an appendix proof never learns
that another found the same quantity treated differently in the main text --
the exact shape of the cross-location findings this harness exists to recover.

With rounds=2, the orchestrator writes a digest of every candidate finding to
the workspace and re-runs each investigator with it, asking what those leads
imply for its own part of the paper. The board carries ids, titles, locations
and one-line claims and nothing of the reasoning or computation behind them,
and it is written by the orchestrator rather than by the agents: an agent
shown another's derivation audits the derivation instead of the paper, which
is the distinction the whole independent-refuter design rests on. The brief
forbids repeating, citing or relying on an entry, and everything the round
produces still passes the independent refuter.

rounds=1 is the default and leaves the existing path untouched, so this is an
A/B rather than a replacement: agent_swarm against agent_swarm_xref in the
eval harness. Whether it actually raises recall without costing precision is
measured next; if it costs precision it comes out.

Also splits the five role agents into coarse/agent/roles.py, which keeps
orchestrator under the size cap. That split matters for _refute in
particular: it is deliberately given the claim and the paper and NOT the
investigator's reasoning, and the omission is easier to see when the function
is not buried in the flow that produced the claim.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: feat(agent): ship --refute for comments only; remove the macro-issue half
highlights.body:
The macro-issue gate was built, measured on three papers, and does not earn
its place. On psi it converted no unsupported issue and dropped a supported
one. On coset_codes its entire upside was two issues flipping to supported
when their narrowed text was re-judged, by a judge already observed to change
verdict on byte-identical text.

Reading the narrowed output settled it. An issue titled 'Multiplicity formulas
rest on unverified uniformity assumptions' came back with a body saying the
assumption 'holds for the partitions checked here ... which reproduces the
table's 44, 252, 764 and 316': the deletion had removed the criticism and left
text confirming the assumption, under a title still asserting the defect. A
gate that can leave a heading contradicting its own paragraph should not run on
an author-facing review.

Removes refute_issues, _refute_issue, narrow_by_deletion and its whitespace
helpers, IssueVerdict, refute_review, the issue-refuter prompt, and their
tests. The pipeline calls refute_comments directly. The overall feedback now
passes through the stage untouched, which a pipeline-level test asserts.

The removed code is in this branch's history if it is worth revisiting with
more papers and a verdict-stable judge.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): report the gate gross, add the coverage check, drop an unsupported claim
highlights.body:
Three corrections to how the result is stated.

The headline was net. Gross it is 9 bad comments dropped, 3 good claims
dropped, and 2 bad issues that became good when their narrowed text was
re-judged — so the macro-issue half's entire upside is two re-judgements by a
judge that has changed verdict on byte-identical text, which is what this
measurement otherwise excludes.

'Keeps the pipeline's coverage' was asserted, not measured. Crossing each
reference finding's matching claim against what the gate did to it: no finding
on any of the three papers was carried by a claim the gate dropped. Eight ride
on a narrowed claim, which re-scoring recall would settle and which has not
been done.

'Making the gate subtractive made it reproducible' is withdrawn. It rested on
two runs compared by counts, the second overwrote the first's per-claim record,
and the comment refuter's prompt and drop rule did not change, so the redesign
cannot be the cause.

Also: the Design bullet for --refute described comments only, the CHANGELOG
still said a comment is rewritten when misstated, and two caveats were missing
(the all-refuted notice is English only; nobody has read a deletion-narrowed
issue end to end).
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(agent): tidy whitespace only at the cut when narrowing an issue
highlights.body:
narrow_by_deletion collapsed whitespace across the whole body, so every
narrowed issue lost its paragraph breaks and the newlines inside display math,
turning it into one run-on block. That damaged the issue whether or not the
deletion itself was right, and 15 of 35 issues across the benchmark papers
were narrowed.

Whitespace is now tidied only where a span was removed: a deletion that
spanned a paragraph boundary keeps the break, one inside a paragraph leaves a
single space, and display math is untouched. Tests cover the paragraph,
inline, display-math, rewrapped and trailing cases.

refute_effect.py now also saves the post-refutation review and each narrowed
issue's before and after text. Nothing was persisting what a narrowed issue
says, so no one could read one for a dangling fragment or a lost antecedent.

Deletes evals/refute_saved.py, which still read the removed rewritten_body
field and would crash.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): final refutation measurement on three papers
highlights.body:
Measured on identical generation with stored verdicts carried forward for
untouched claims, reported as good and bad counts under the stricter
supported-and-substantive test.

Across psi, the held-out coset_codes, and targeting: 11 bad claims removed
against 1 good one lost, at about $1.85 a paper.

Three findings that matter more than the total, and one of them reverses this
document's previous claim:

- The comment half carries the benefit (9 bad removed, 2 good lost). The
  macro-issue half is marginal (2 bad removed, 1 good gained) and was net
  negative on psi, converting no bad issue and dropping a good one. The
  earlier claim that the issue half 'mattered most' came from the retracted
  measurements and does not survive them.
- On targeting, the only paper no design decision here has touched and whose
  review was already 26 good to 6 bad, the gate dropped nothing and changed no
  verdict. The right failure mode, but it means the value depends on the paper.
- Making the gate subtractive made it reproducible: two genuine psi runs agree
  exactly, where the rewriting version dropped 4, then 5, then 6 of the same
  comments.

The recommendation stays opt-in, and now names the macro-issue half as the
open question rather than the main gain.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): withdraw the refutation figures and record why they were wrong
highlights.body:
Three successive attempts at what the gate is worth were each wrong: comparing
two different pipeline runs, re-judging unchanged text through a judge that
drifts, and scoring an is-this-supported test that a hedged rewrite satisfies.
The third changed the design rather than the measurement.

The doc now states the withdrawal, the three mistakes, and the shape that
survived all of them, rather than a number. It no longer recommends
considering --refute as a default.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(agent): make the refutation gate purely subtractive
highlights.body:
Reading the saved reviews showed the gate was rewriting the review, not
verifying it, and that this was the source of its own measured gain.

Issues: asking for a replacement body produced a rewrite longer than the
original on every narrowed issue across both benchmark papers (1.0x to 1.6x),
each prefixed with the issue title. Refusing those by length left the issue
half drop-only, which pays nothing; accepting them made an agent the author of
review prose. Narrowing is now expressed as deletion: the refuter names
verbatim spans of the body that the paper does not bear out, and the code
removes them, so every surviving word is the reviewer's own. Matching is exact
then whitespace-insensitive, since a model re-wraps a sentence it quotes; a
span that still does not match removes nothing, so a hallucinated span cannot
alter the issue, and naming every span drops the issue outright.

Comments: corrected_claim is no longer applied. Sampling the rewrites found
ones that retreated from 'X is wrong' to 'the paper does not say how X was
handled', which satisfies an is-this-supported test while giving the author
less -- so part of the measured precision gain was an artefact of the metric.
The suggestion stays on the verdict for a human to weigh. severity is now only
ever lowered: the field defaults to 'major', so applying it unconditionally
raised the severity of comments the refuter never reconsidered.

Because the gate now only removes, every surviving comment keeps the verdict
already stored for it and the effect measurement needs no re-judging except
for narrowed issue bodies. refute_effect.py reports good and bad counts rather
than rates, and records per-claim what the gate did.

Refutation tests move to tests/test_agent_refutation.py beside their module.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(agent): make narrowing actually narrow, and key comments by position
highlights.body:
Three defects, two of them found by reading the saved reviews rather than the
verdicts.

refute_comments keyed its lookup maps on comment.number. This stage runs
before _renumber_comments, so the numbers are whatever the editorial pass
emitted, and on the double-failure fallback path they are raw section order
with section-local numbering where duplicates are expected. Comments sharing a
number collapsed the maps and had verdicts misattributed. Keyed on position
now, as the issue path already was.

Every narrowed issue body on the benchmark papers came back LONGER than the
one it replaced, against the prompt's explicit instruction to say less and
never more, and each began by repeating the issue title so the rendered review
showed the title twice. A prompt cannot enforce either. _clean_narrowed_body
strips a repeated title and refuses a body that does not shorten, keeping the
original instead: a rewrite that expands makes this stage an author of review
content rather than a verifier of it, which is the risk the ledger link
elsewhere exists to prevent.

The review language now reaches both refuters. A refuter writes author-facing
prose (corrected_claim, rewritten_body), and the issue refuter rewrites most
of what it touches, so without this the rewrite came back in English inside a
localized review. The all-issues-refuted notice is still English; that is
recorded as a caveat.

Adds a pipeline-level test for review_paper(refute=True), which the benchmark
never exercised because it called refute_comments and refute_issues directly.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): measure the refutation gate on identical generation
highlights.body:
refute_saved.py now also refutes the macro issues and can save what survives
as its own run, so precision before and after is compared on the same
generation rather than across two pipeline runs.

With both halves refuted, on psi and on the held-out coset_codes: unsupported
claims halve (10 to 4, and 16 to 8), precision rises 19 and 17 points, recall
is unchanged on one paper and loses one finding of 25 on the other, and the
pass costs about $1.85. Issue precision, the gap the comment-only version
left at 58% and 36%, reaches 80% and 50%.

The per-claim cross-tabulation shows why the two halves need separate
contracts: the gate drops 8 of 14 false comments for 2 of 25 good ones, while
on issues it narrows 12 of 23 rather than dropping them, and the narrowed text
is what the precision gain is measured on. Two caveats are stated with it: the
refuter has real run-to-run variance, and it also narrowed 6 issues the judge
had called supported, so the trade is net positive on these two papers rather
than free.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: feat(agent): refute the macro issues too, narrowing rather than dropping
highlights.body:
With comments alone refuted, comment precision reached 94% and 100% on the two
benchmark papers while macro-issue precision stayed at 58% and 36%, so every
surviving unsupported claim was in the overall feedback.

A macro issue is not a comment and needs a different contract. It carries no
verbatim anchor, so the refuter locates the passages itself. And it bundles
several points under one theme, so the common outcome is that some hold and
some do not: dropping a four-point issue because its third point is answered
in Section 6 discards three good ones, while keeping it whole ships the wrong
one. IssueVerdict therefore adds 'partly_supported', which replaces the body
with the reviewer's narrowed version and records what was dropped and where
the paper answers it. The title survives narrowing.

Guards: an issue is kept unchanged when the check could not run or came back
inconclusive, so neither an infrastructure failure nor honest uncertainty
deletes one; a narrowing with no replacement text keeps the original, since
the reviewer called it partly right; and if every issue is refuted, an
explicit notice replaces them rather than reinstating the least-bad one,
because OverviewFeedback requires an issue and the least-bad one is still a
claim the paper contradicts.

refute_review is now the single entry point the pipeline stage calls, with the
two halves failing independently so a failure in one leaves the other verified.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: refactor(agent): split the pipeline-facing refutation gate into its own module
highlights.body:
orchestrator.py reached 804 lines, over the architecture cap. refute_comments
is the natural seam: orchestrator holds the roles and modes, refutation holds
the gate applied to comments produced outside them, which the measurement made
the primary use. 702 and 127 lines.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix: validate the agent mode, and don't drop a substantive 'Funding' section
highlights.body:
run_agentic_review fell through to swarm for any unrecognized mode, so a typo
in --agent silently ran a different and dearer mode; it now raises.

Section eligibility skipped any title starting with a boilerplate word, which
would discard an economics paper's 'Funding and acquisition dynamics in
venture capital'. The prefix test now applies only to headings short enough to
be that boilerplate.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): rewrite from the paired refutation measurement
highlights.body:
The refutation result was unpaired: pipeline_refuted was a separate pipeline
run, so comparing it with the pipeline arm compared two different reviews.
evals/refute_saved.py now runs the refuter over the exact comments the judge
already adjudicated, one paired observation per comment. The honest figure is
much smaller than the one that was published here: comment precision 64% to
82% across the two papers, the gate dropping 9 of 14 false criticisms and 2 of
25 good ones, and the two papers differing a great deal.

Also: the design section listed two tools that do not exist (web_search,
finding_write) and omitted that there is no web search and only one refutation
pass; the tool-judge result is now described as consistent with the diagnosis
rather than confirming it, since its prompt names the hypothesis; the host
isolation section no longer describes a particular machine's configuration;
and a closing section states plainly where the work departs from what was
asked.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs: correct module descriptions and the section-fix changelog entry
highlights.body:
The seven module descriptions added to the package-structure tables were
written from the file names rather than from the modules. Checked against each
docstring: handoff_url only parses (it does not construct, and nothing is
signed), native_runtime suspends model calls as native tasks and replays
validated responses rather than detecting and launching a runtime, and
native_review and review_runtime were also inaccurate. All seven now follow
their docstrings.

The changelog claimed the fix makes the pipeline review every section. It does
not: the cap still binds on a long paper, and the entry now says which
sections are dropped and that the choice is logged.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(agent): enforce sandbox network denial at the OS level
highlights.body:
The 'no network' claim was false. Denial was a Python-level patch of the
socket module, and two one-liners defeated it: subprocess shelling out to
/usr/bin/curl returned HTTP 200, and 'import _socket' connected directly,
since the patch only touches the pure-Python wrapper. A paper is untrusted
input, so a prompt-injected paper that induced the model to write an
exfiltrating check would have had a working path out.

Denial now comes from the OS where a mechanism exists: sandbox-exec with a
deny-network seatbelt profile on macOS, 'unshare --net' on Linux where
permitted. Both are probed by actually running them, because either can be
present and refuse. Verified on this host: the curl bypass now exits 6 and
_socket cannot connect, while sympy still imports and runs.

Where no mechanism is available there is no network bound, and nothing now
claims otherwise: available_isolation() reports the mechanism, and the python
tool's description is generated from it, so a host without isolation tells the
model so instead of giving it a false assurance. The socket patch stays as a
legible error message rather than a bound, and both bypasses are now tests.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): final arm comparison, with a tool-using second adjudication
highlights.body:
Adds the refuted-pipeline arms, which validate the recommendation: refutation
took detailed-comment precision from 58% to 100% on the held-out paper and
from 70% to 94% on the other. It also shows where the remaining false
criticism is — entirely in the macro issues, which the stage does not yet
refute.

Adds evals/adjudicate.py, a second audit by a judge with the same workspace
and tools the agents get, because the single-prompt judge never abstained and
was being asked to check lookups it had no means to perform. It is more
lenient, so the single-prompt precision figures were too harsh and are now
reported alongside it. It confirms the mechanism far more firmly: five of the
six unsupported claims it found are objections the paper answers elsewhere,
and it names the location each time.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: chore(evals): keep benchmark inputs out of the repository
highlights.body:
structure.json embeds the whole paper text while paper.md was ignored, which
was an inconsistent policy for the same content, and the reference reviews are
third-party documents. evals/papers/ is now ignored in full. What stays
committed is the atomized finding sets under evals/references/ and
prepare_paper.py, which regenerates the rest from a local PDF.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: docs(agent): full arm comparison across two papers, with the leakage caveat
highlights.body:
Replaces the single-paper table with both papers and all arms, and states the
leakage plainly: the role prompts were written after reading the first paper's
reference review and name the patterns it found, so recall on that paper is
in-sample and the held-out paper is the honest measurement.

The recommendation follows what was measured rather than the premise the
branch started from: the staged pipeline leads on coverage and asserts the
most unsupported claims, the agent arms reverse both, so verification is added
to the generator instead of replacing it.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: feat(pipeline): add --refute, an independent re-check of every comment
highlights.body:
The arm comparison measured generation and verification as complements, not
substitutes. On both benchmark papers the staged pipeline was the coverage
leader and also asserted the most claims the paper does not support: 15 of 32
on one, 16 of 31 on the other, roughly half. The agent arms reversed both,
asserting almost nothing unsupported while finding far too little.

So rather than replacing the staged pipeline, refute_comments applies the
agent runtime's gate to the comments it already produced. Each one goes to a
fresh-context agent that sees the claim and its quote, has tool access to the
whole paper, and must reproduce the defect; a comment it cannot reproduce is
dropped, and one that is real but misstated is rewritten from the refuter's
corrected claim. A comment whose check could not run is kept, so an
infrastructure failure never silently deletes a finding.

Exposed as review_paper(refute=True) and 'coarse review --refute', off by
default, with a pipeline_refuted evaluation arm.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: feat(cli): add --agent to run a review through the bounded agent runtime
highlights.body:
Until now the agent runtime had no entry point: review_paper always ran the
staged pipeline, so the whole package was unreachable from the CLI or the
library. review_paper takes agent_mode (sweep|swarm|single) and `coarse
review --agent <mode>` sets it. Default None, so the staged path is
unchanged.

The agent branch reuses the shared quote verifier and renderer rather than
its own, so the verbatim-quote guarantee is identical on both paths; a test
covers that a fabricated quote is still dropped from an agent review.

pipeline.py joins the oversized-module allowlist at 880 lines. Moving the
quote-repair helpers to review_stages.py would have kept it under the cap but
broke 22 tests that patch those names on coarse.pipeline, so that refactor
belongs in its own change rather than riding along here.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: chore(tests): record the prompts.py cap bump for the sweep brief
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: feat(agent): add sweep mode — broad coverage behind the refutation gate
highlights.body:
Measured separately on the benchmark paper, the two capabilities were
complementary rather than competing. A single full-paper pass reached nine of
sixteen reference findings but asserted one the paper does not support. The
role swarm asserted nothing unsupported across three runs, and reached two
appendix findings nothing else reached (a one-sided premise in a composition
lemma, and a curvature bound off by a factor of two), but only three to five
findings in total: narrow targets do not cover a paper.

Sweep divides every reviewable section into contiguous regions, one per
investigator, and briefs each for breadth rather than for a single question --
same demonstration bar, but abstention is no longer the expected outcome. Every
candidate still passes through an independent fresh-context refuter before the
editor sees it. The brief also tells a sweeper to search the rest of the paper
before reporting that something is missing, which is the failure that produced
every unsupported comment in the pipeline arm.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(agent): require the planner to name at least one target
highlights.body:
The planner submitted an empty plan on every run, after seven turns and ten
of its thirty-five permitted tool calls, so it was not running out of budget:
InvestigationPlan simply allowed an empty list, and an empty submission
validated. The orchestrator then fell back to structural targets and the
LLM plan was never used.

An empty plan is never a useful answer, unlike an empty FindingBatch where
abstention is the point. Requiring a target makes the empty submission fail
validation, which the runner already feeds back to the agent as a rejection
to repair.

Also adds evals/prepare_paper.py, which extracts a held-out paper, analyzes
its structure and atomizes its reference review mechanically (one finding per
macro issue and per detailed comment). Needed because the role prompts were
written after reading the first paper's reference review and name the patterns
that review found, so recall on that paper is in-sample and cannot support a
quality claim on its own.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(agent,evals): enforce the ledger link in code and audit macro issues too
highlights.body:
Two measurement and safety gaps the first arm comparison exposed.

The editor was told to write only from confirmed findings but nothing checked
it. Each detailed comment now carries the finding id it reports, and a comment
whose id is not in the confirmed set is dropped, so a finding an independent
refuter did not reproduce cannot re-enter the report through the editor. When
the editor attributes nothing at all the comments are kept and the degradation
is logged, rather than discarding a whole report over a missing field.

Precision was adjudicated over detailed comments only while recall credited
macro issues as well, so an arm that put its claims in the overall feedback
was credited for hits and never charged for misses. On the benchmark paper
that asymmetry mattered a great deal: the whole of one arm's measured recall
came from its macro issues and none of its 21 detailed comments matched a
reference finding. Both halves of a review are now adjudicated, and recall
reports how many hits came from a detailed comment rather than only from a
macro issue.
highlights.author: David Van Dijcke

highlights.message: fix(pipeline): keep a proof whose title the heading parser mangled
highlights.body:
Section eligibility filtered on the title, dropping any section titled
`<!-- PAGE BREAK -->`. When a page break falls immediately before a heading
the parser uses the marker as the title and leaves the real heading in the
body, so such a section can hold real content: on the benchmark paper one is
1,107 characters of "A.6 Proof of Theorem 2", the proof of the paper's
central result, and the reference review's critical finding is about a step
in it.

Eligibility is now judged on the text alone. The underlying mis-titling in
structure.py is untouched.

highlights.body:
The pipeline matched a plain one-prompt baseline's recall while emitting seven
criticisms the adjudicator found unsupported, and all seven fail for the same
reason: the objection is answered elsewhere in the paper, where a
single-section prompt cannot see it.

highlights.message: Download limits, first part of #699: no download path without a limit; ResearchBox held to the limits; GEO, ENA and ArrayExpress records whose archive did not answer are "unreachable", not "unfound". Version 0.4.4.28
highlights.body:

A code file inside an archive is no longer requested from the address "NA" with download = FALSE.
- reproducibility_check passes max_file_size and max_download_size to the code_check it runs.
- .tar_fetch_members() stops an archive of unknown size at what is left of the budget.
- ResearchBox: repo_check (and data_check and code_check, which pass them on) and rbox_file_download() have max_file_size and max_download_size. With an API key the file list is asked first and only the smallest files up to the budget are downloaded; without a key the download stops at the budget and the box is reported as not downloaded. .download_capped() takes a prepared request.
- The message about files over max_file_size rounds the largest size up to 0.1 MB.
- seq_archive_info(): .seq_fetch() tells an archive that did not answer from one that has no such record.
- Documentation corrected: a file of unknown size is downloaded up to a limit, not skipped; osf_file_download()'s default mode is "all", without limits; download_repo_files()'s budget counts only the files of one call.
